Build triggers (B) start builds based on source events. Build notifications (C) send alerts about build status but do not gate execution on human decisions.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Approvers are specified via IAM roles (cloudbuild.builds.approve permission), and approval requests can be routed to specific teams or individuals based on the trigger or pipeline configuration.
  • Builds waiting for approval have a configurable timeout window (default 24 hours); if no approval or rejection is received before the timeout, the build is automatically canceled.
  • Rejection cancels the build with an optional reason message that is recorded in build history, providing an audit trail of who rejected what and why for compliance purposes.
  • Approval gates are commonly combined with Cloud Deploy promotion approvals to create a multi-layer governance model: Cloud Build gates the build artifact creation, and Cloud Deploy gates the deployment to each environment.

questions.title: Pub/Sub Dead Letter Topics
questions.scenario: Messages that repeatedly fail processing should be moved to a separate topic for investigation rather than blocking the queue or being lost.
questions.questionText: Which Pub/Sub feature captures messages that cannot be processed after multiple retries?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Pub/Sub can redirect messages that fail processing after a configurable number of delivery attempts to a separate topic, preventing poison messages from blocking the main subscription.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Dead letter topics in Pub/Sub capture messages that cannot be successfully acknowledged after a specified number of delivery attempts. This prevents poison messages from blocking healthy message processing and preserves them for later investigation and reprocessing. Message retention (A) keeps acknowledged messages available for replay but does not handle failures. Message filtering (B) routes messages based on attributes at subscription time, not based on processing failures. Snapshot restore (D) resets a subscription to a previous point in time but does not isolate failed messages.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Maximum delivery attempts is configurable per subscription (range 5 to 100); after exceeding this threshold, the message is forwarded to the dead letter topic with metadata indicating the original subscription and delivery attempt count.
  • Dead-lettered messages retain their original attributes and payload, plus Pub/Sub adds a CloudPubSubDeadLetterSourceSubscription attribute so consumers can identify which subscription produced the failure.
  • Monitoring the dead letter topic's message count and publish rate with Cloud Monitoring alerts enables teams to detect processing failures early, before they accumulate into a backlog.
  • A common operational pattern is to create a pull subscription on the dead letter topic, periodically review failed messages, fix the processing bug, and then replay messages back to the original topic for reprocessing.

questions.title: Managed Service for Prometheus
questions.scenario: A team uses Prometheus for metrics collection but wants to reduce operational burden while maintaining compatibility with existing Prometheus queries and Grafana dashboards.
questions.questionText: Which Google Cloud service provides fully managed, Prometheus-compatible metrics collection?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Google Cloud offers a fully managed Prometheus-compatible backend that ingests metrics from existing Prometheus exporters and supports PromQL queries without running your own Prometheus server.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Managed Service for Prometheus (part of Cloud Monitoring) provides a globally scalable, Prometheus-compatible metrics backend managed by Google. Teams keep their existing Prometheus instrumentation, exporters, and PromQL queries while offloading storage, scaling, and operations. Cloud Monitoring (A) is the broader platform that includes Managed Prometheus but uses its own query language (MQL) by default, not PromQL. Cloud Trace (C) handles distributed tracing, not metrics. Prometheus on GKE (D) is self-managed Prometheus, which is exactly the operational burden the team wants to eliminate.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Managed Service for Prometheus supports both managed collection (Google deploys and manages the collector) and self-deployed collection (you run the collector with Google's remote-write endpoint as the storage backend).
  • PromQL queries work with minimal modification, and existing Grafana dashboards that query Prometheus can be pointed at the managed backend by updating the data source URL to the Google-managed frontend.
  • Metrics stored in Managed Prometheus are available alongside native Cloud Monitoring metrics, enabling unified dashboards and alerting policies that combine both Prometheus and GCP infrastructure metrics.
  • Global replication ensures high availability and durability of metrics data; unlike self-hosted Prometheus, there is no single-node storage bottleneck or risk of data loss from pod eviction or disk failure.

questions.title: Skaffold Integration
questions.scenario: Developers want a tool that handles building, pushing, and deploying applications during local development with the same configuration used in CI/CD.
questions.questionText: Which tool provides continuous development for Kubernetes with Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy integration?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The tool you need manages the full build-push-deploy lifecycle for Kubernetes applications, with native integration to both Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy for consistent local and CI/CD workflows.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Skaffold is an open-source command-line tool by Google that automates the build, push, and deploy workflow for Kubernetes applications. It integrates natively with Cloud Build for remote builds and Cloud Deploy for production delivery. Helm (A) is a package manager for Kubernetes that templates manifests but does not manage the build-push-deploy loop. kubectl (B) is the Kubernetes CLI for applying manifests. Kustomize (C) generates Kubernetes manifests through overlay composition but does not handle building or pushing container images.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• skaffold.yaml defines build, test, and deploy configurations in a single file; Cloud Deploy uses the same skaffold.yaml to render and deploy manifests, ensuring development and production use identical deployment logic.
  • File sync enables rapid inner-loop iteration by syncing changed source files directly into running containers, avoiding full image rebuilds for interpreted languages like Python and Node.js.
  • Profiles in skaffold.yaml support different configurations for dev, staging, and production, such as using local Docker builds for development and Cloud Build for CI, all switchable via a command-line flag.
  • Skaffold's dev mode watches for file changes and automatically rebuilds, pushes, and redeploys the application, providing a hot-reload development experience for Kubernetes-native applications.

questions.title: BigQuery Materialized Views
questions.scenario: A complex aggregation query runs frequently and always produces the same results for the same input data. The team wants to avoid recomputing it every time.
questions.questionText: Which BigQuery feature automatically precomputes and caches query results that update incrementally?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: BigQuery has a feature that stores precomputed aggregation results, updates them incrementally as base data changes, and automatically rewrites matching queries to use the cached results.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Materialized views in BigQuery precompute and cache the results of a query definition. When base table data changes, only the delta is recomputed and applied incrementally. BigQuery's smart tuning automatically rewrites queries that match the view's pattern to use the cached results. Scheduled queries (A) run SQL on a timer but do not integrate with query optimization. Query cache (C) stores results of identical queries but expires when base data changes. Table snapshots (D) capture point-in-time table state for backup, not query acceleration.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Smart tuning automatically detects when a user's query can be satisfied by a materialized view and rewrites the execution plan to read from the cached results, even if the user did not explicitly reference the view.
  • Materialized views can be refreshed automatically (BigQuery manages the refresh interval) or manually via the REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW statement, giving teams control over freshness versus cost trade-offs.
  • Materialized views incur storage costs for the cached data, but the compute savings from avoiding repeated full-table aggregation scans typically outweigh the storage cost for frequently queried patterns.
  • Materialized views support aggregation functions (SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, MAX), filters, GROUP BY, and INNER JOIN, covering the most common dashboard and reporting query patterns.

questions.title: Eventarc
questions.scenario: A service needs to automatically trigger when specific events occur in Google Cloud, such as when files are uploaded to Cloud Storage or when Pub/Sub messages arrive.
questions.questionText: Which Google Cloud service provides event-driven architecture by routing events to targets like Cloud Run?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The service you need is a centralized event routing layer that connects events from GCP services, Pub/Sub, and third parties to targets like Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, and Workflows.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Eventarc is a fully managed event routing service that connects event sources (GCP services, Pub/Sub, third-party providers) to event handlers (Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, Workflows) using declarative triggers. Pub/Sub (A) is a messaging layer that Eventarc uses as transport but does not provide the trigger-routing abstraction. Cloud Functions (C) can be an event target but is not an event routing service itself. Cloud Scheduler (D) triggers actions on a timer, not in response to system events.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Event triggers define a source, event type filter, and target destination; for example, a trigger can fire when a specific Cloud Storage bucket receives an object.finalize event and route it to a Cloud Run service.
  • Eventarc uses the CloudEvents specification (CNCF standard) for event format, providing a consistent, vendor-neutral envelope structure with type, source, subject, and data fields.
  • Audit Log event triggers enable reacting to any audited GCP API call, such as creating a Compute Engine instance or modifying an IAM policy, making virtually any GCP action an event source.
  • Eventarc Advanced supports cross-project and cross-region event routing with message buses, enabling enterprise-scale event architectures where producers and consumers span multiple GCP projects.

questions.title: Service Mesh Observability
questions.scenario: A microservices application running on GKE needs automatic mTLS, traffic management, and observability without modifying application code.
questions.questionText: Which GKE feature provides service mesh capabilities with built-in observability?

choices.text: Anthos Service Mesh (or Cloud Service Mesh)

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The GKE feature you need provides a managed Istio-based service mesh that handles mTLS encryption, traffic routing, and telemetry collection via sidecar proxies without application code changes.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Anthos Service Mesh (also called Cloud Service Mesh) is a managed Istio-based service mesh that provides mutual TLS encryption, traffic management, and observability for microservices on GKE. It automatically collects telemetry and provides topology dashboards without code modifications. GKE Ingress (B) manages external HTTP/S traffic routing to services but does not provide service-to-service encryption, traffic splitting, or mesh-level observability. Cloud Load Balancing (C) distributes traffic at the infrastructure level. Cloud Armor (D) provides WAF and DDoS protection for external endpoints.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Envoy sidecar proxies are injected alongside each application container and handle all inbound and outbound traffic transparently, providing mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, and telemetry without any application code changes.
  • Service-level SLOs can be defined and monitored directly in the Cloud Service Mesh dashboard, showing error rates, latency percentiles, and availability against configured targets for each service.
  • Traffic splitting enables canary deployments and A/B testing at the mesh level by routing a configurable percentage of requests to different service versions based on HTTP headers, weights, or other criteria.
  • The service topology graph provides a real-time visualization of service dependencies, request rates, error rates, and latency between services, making it easy to identify the blast radius of a failing service.

questions.title: Secret Manager Integration
questions.scenario: A Cloud Build pipeline needs to access database credentials securely without storing them in the repository or build configuration.
questions.questionText: Which Google Cloud service should be used to securely store and access secrets in CI/CD pipelines?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Google Cloud provides a dedicated service for storing, versioning, and accessing sensitive data like API keys, passwords, and certificates, with native Cloud Build integration via the availableSecrets field.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Secret Manager is Google Cloud's secure storage service for API keys, passwords, certificates, and other sensitive data. Cloud Build accesses secrets using the availableSecrets field in cloudbuild.yaml, which injects them as environment variables or mounted files during build execution. Cloud KMS (B) manages encryption keys for encrypting and decrypting data but is not designed for storing secret values directly. IAM (C) controls who can access resources but does not store secrets. Config Connector (D) manages GCP resources via Kubernetes CRDs, not secret storage.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Secrets are versioned automatically: each update creates a new version, enabling rotation strategies where new versions are deployed gradually while old versions remain accessible for rollback.
  • IAM policies control access at both the secret level and the version level, so you can grant a service account access to only the latest version while restricting access to historical versions for audit purposes.
  • Automatic replication policies (user-managed or automatic) replicate secret data across specified regions, ensuring high availability and enabling low-latency access from any region where your workloads run.
  • Secret Manager integrates with Pub/Sub notifications to fire events on secret version creation, rotation, or deletion, enabling automated workflows like restarting services when credentials are rotated.

gl-cloud-build.name: Cloud Build
gl-cloud-build.definition: A fully managed CI/CD platform that executes builds on Google Cloud infrastructure using customizable build steps defined in YAML.
gl-cloud-build.examNote: Cloud Build uses cloudbuild.yaml for configuration and supports triggers for automated builds.

gl-cloud-deploy.name: Cloud Deploy
gl-cloud-deploy.definition: A managed continuous delivery service that automates the deployment of applications to GKE, Cloud Run, and other targets with approval gates and rollback support.
gl-cloud-deploy.examNote: Use Cloud Deploy for progressive delivery with promotion between dev, staging, and production targets.

gl-artifact-registry.name: Artifact Registry
gl-artifact-registry.definition: A universal artifact management service that stores Docker images, language packages (npm, Maven, Python), and OS packages with integrated vulnerability scanning.
gl-artifact-registry.examNote: Artifact Registry is the recommended replacement for Container Registry with additional format support.

gl-bigquery.name: BigQuery
gl-bigquery.definition: A serverless, highly scalable enterprise data warehouse that enables SQL queries on petabytes of data with separation of storage and compute.
gl-bigquery.examNote: BigQuery supports partitioning, clustering, and BigQuery ML for machine learning with SQL.

gl-dataflow.name: Dataflow
gl-dataflow.definition: A fully managed service for executing Apache Beam pipelines that provides unified batch and stream data processing with automatic scaling.
gl-dataflow.examNote: Dataflow provides exactly-once processing semantics and supports templates for reusable pipelines.

gl-dataproc.name: Dataproc
gl-dataproc.definition: A managed Spark and Hadoop service that enables running open-source data analytics workloads with fast cluster creation and autoscaling.
gl-dataproc.examNote: Dataproc Serverless runs Spark jobs without cluster management.

gl-pubsub.name: Pub/Sub
gl-pubsub.definition: A global, real-time messaging service that decouples services by allowing asynchronous communication through topics and subscriptions.
gl-pubsub.examNote: Pub/Sub supports both push and pull delivery modes with at-least-once or exactly-once semantics.

gl-cloud-composer.name: Cloud Composer
gl-cloud-composer.definition: A fully managed workflow orchestration service built on Apache Airflow that allows authoring, scheduling, and monitoring data pipelines using Python DAGs.
gl-cloud-composer.examNote: Use Cloud Composer for complex data pipelines; use Cloud Workflows for simpler orchestration.

gl-dag.name: DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph)
gl-dag.definition: A collection of tasks with dependencies that defines the execution order in Apache Airflow, where the acyclic property ensures no circular dependencies.
gl-dag.examNote: DAGs are defined in Python and uploaded to the Cloud Composer DAGs folder.

gl-cloud-monitoring.name: Cloud Monitoring
gl-cloud-monitoring.definition: A service that collects metrics, events, and metadata from Google Cloud resources, enabling dashboards, alerting, and uptime monitoring.
gl-cloud-monitoring.examNote: Cloud Monitoring supports SLO monitoring and includes Managed Service for Prometheus.

gl-cloud-logging.name: Cloud Logging
gl-cloud-logging.definition: A fully managed service for storing, searching, analyzing, and alerting on log data from Google Cloud and custom sources.
gl-cloud-logging.examNote: Use log sinks to route logs to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, or Pub/Sub.

gl-binary-auth.name: Binary Authorization
gl-binary-auth.definition: A deploy-time security control that ensures only trusted container images are deployed based on attestations (cryptographic signatures).
gl-binary-auth.examNote: Binary Authorization integrates with Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning.

gl-secret-manager.name: Secret Manager
gl-secret-manager.definition: A secure storage service for API keys, passwords, certificates, and other sensitive data with versioning, access control, and automatic replication.
gl-secret-manager.examNote: Cloud Build can inject secrets from Secret Manager as environment variables.

gl-error-budget.name: Error Budget
gl-error-budget.definition: The inverse of an SLO that represents the maximum amount of unreliability (downtime or errors) allowed before breaching the service level objective.
gl-error-budget.examNote: Error budgets help balance reliability with feature velocity in SRE practices.

gl-canary.name: Canary Deployment
gl-canary.definition: A deployment strategy that releases changes to a small subset of users before rolling out to the entire infrastructure, enabling early detection of issues.
gl-canary.examNote: Cloud Deploy supports canary deployments with configurable traffic percentages.
